summary: A draft of IPng requirements from the point of view of the Cellular Digital Packet Data consortium of service providers. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A group that sends data over cell phone networks says what it needs from the next Internet.

subtitle: Wireless carrier networks want mobility, scalability, and reliable accounting built into IPng.

tldr.problem: Cellular data networks need features that the current Internet was not designed for: mobile devices, vast address space, and billing.
tldr.mechanism: IPng should support native mobility (not just tunnels), hierarchical addresses, security, Layer 3 accounting, source-based routing for carrier choice, and efficient bandwidth use.
tldr.outcome: Mobile data networks can offer seamless service as devices move, while maintaining clear billing and carrier selection, with IP as the underlying layer.

today: RFC 1674 is Informational from August 1994. IPv6 eventually included mechanisms for mobility (via IPv6 mobility support protocols) and was adopted by cellular carriers. However, IPv6 mobility has remained optional and complex; most mobile networks use tunneling and other techniques rather than native IPng mobility as the RFC envisioned.

sections.title: The Cellular Digital Packet Data Perspective
sections.content:
RFC 1674 presents the view of the Cellular Digital Packet Data (CDPD) consortium, a group of wireless service providers. Mark Taylor from McCaw Cellular explains that as leading providers of nascent mobile data technology, the consortium is committed to supporting whatever form IPng takes, but has several critical requirements.

The RFC frames IPng as an opportunity to design in features for mobility from the start, rather than bolting them on later. The statement represents input for technical discussions but not a commitment from the industry or individual companies.
sections.plainLanguage: Wireless carriers say they will use whatever IPng becomes, but they want it designed for phones and mobile devices from the start.

sections.title: Mobility and Scale
sections.content:
The primary requirement is that IPng must not impede mobile devices. IPng must allow devices to operate anywhere anytime, with applications looking and feeling the same regardless of location. NPDUs (network protocol data units) must be self-contained and support redirection; IPng must be connectionless.

CDPD projects 20 to 40 million North American users by 2007 (each could be a vending machine or a road warrior) and billions worldwide. IPng must support tens or hundreds of billions of addresses to account for the sparseness required by subnetting. The consortium also highlights the need to support occasionally-connected hosts that go offline and rejoin.
sections.plainLanguage: Phones should work anywhere, even moving between towers. The system should handle billions of devices and not break when a phone goes offline and comes back.

sections.title: Addressing, Security, and Efficiency
sections.content:
IPng addresses should be hierarchical for scalable routing. A node with multiple links should be addressable by a single address (though multiple addresses should also be allowed). Address-to-name mapping should be independent of location: an address is an address, not a route. Variable-length addressing ensures continued protocol extensibility, and address administration should be distributed, not centralized.

Security mechanisms must support peer authentication, data confidentiality, traffic flow confidentiality, data integrity and location confidentiality. Layer 3 accounting is a requirement, following the CDPD model. Policy-based routing and source-based routing should let carriers offer equal access and choice of carrier (comparable to telephone interexchange choice).

Data efficiency is critical since wireless bandwidth is precious. Protocol overhead should be minimized, and packet prioritization (class and grade of service) should be supported.
sections.plainLanguage: Addresses should nest like postal codes; security should hide location; the network should track who to bill; routing should let carriers compete; and every bit counts on slow wireless links.

sections.title: Transition and Coexistence
sections.content:
IPng must interoperate with IPv4 for the foreseeable future. Bridging mechanisms must be supported, and a clear transition strategy from IPv4 to IPng must be defined. Option fields and other mechanisms should allow IPng protocols to support IPv4 addresses and headers where necessary.

This requirement acknowledges the reality that wireless infrastructure will grow alongside existing wired networks for years, requiring dual-stack or translation capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: Old Internet and new Internet must work together for a long time, so people can migrate at their own pace.

references.text: Gross, P. (ed.), "Internet Next Generation Architecture", RFC 1550, December 1993.
